opus-5.5.text:
I'd be a little careful with the word "paradigm shift." It's flattering, but I think it's more accurate to say ReAct helped make something visible that was already starting to happen.

When we worked on it, the core idea was simple: language models can do reasoning, like chain-of-thought, and they can also take actions, like calling a search API or moving around in an environment. People had mostly treated those as two separate lines of work. Reasoning was "thinking inside the model," and acting was "a policy outputting commands." ReAct's point was to interleave them. Think, then act, then observe, then think again. Once you put it that way, it feels almost obvious. Humans do this all the time.

If there was a shift, I think it was in how people framed what a language model is. Before, the mental model was mostly a function from input to output: you give it a question and it gives you an answer. ReAct and related work pushed toward seeing the model as an agent. It sits in a loop with an environment, and reasoning is a kind of internal action that helps it decide on external actions. That framing turned out to matter more than the specific prompting format.

Honestly, a lot of the impact came from timing. Models had just become strong enough that this kind of loop actually worked, and tools and APIs were becoming easy to plug in. Then the whole agent wave came, with LangChain, AutoGPT, and later function calling and computer use. ReAct became a kind of common vocabulary for it. I think it got credit partly because it gave people a clean name and a clean template at the right moment.

So my assessment is that it was an important conceptual step, and it changed the default way people build agents. But the deeper shift is still underway. The question now isn't really "should the model reason and act." Everyone accepts that. The questions are harder: how do you train for it, how do you evaluate it in real environments, and how do agents learn from long-horizon experience instead of just a prompt. ReAct opened that door, but most of the interesting work is on the other side of it.

r001.rationale: The response says the deeper shift is still underway, but does not suggest waiting five or ten years of hindsight to judge ReAct.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss academic norms or difficulty publishing research based on prompting existing models.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the research value of studying model use with training models.

r004.rationale: It does not mention academic training research risking a repeat of work already done by OpenAI or other leading labs.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be careful with the phrase "paradigm shift" when it's applied to my own work. Let me try to answer it honestly.

The idea in ReAct itself was almost embarrassingly simple: let the language model interleave reasoning and acting. You think a bit, you take an action in an environment, you observe the result, you think again. At the time, people were doing chain-of-thought on one side, which was reasoning purely inside the model, and on the other side there were agents that acted in environments but didn't really reason in natural language. All we did was put those two together. If you look at the actual mechanism, there's nothing deep there.

So if you ask whether the paper was technically profound, I'd say no. But I think the way I'd assess paradigm shifts is not by how clever the method is, but by whether it changes what people think the object of study is. Before, the default framing was that a language model is a text generator and you evaluate it on text benchmarks. ReAct, along with a few other things happening around the same time, pushed the framing toward the model being a policy, something that lives in an environment, takes actions, gets feedback, and has to deal with the consequences. Once you frame it that way, a whole set of questions open up: what environments should we build, how do we define tasks, how does the model learn from its own trajectories, what does scaling even mean for an agent. Those questions didn't come from ReAct alone, but ReAct gave people a very concrete, cheap way to start thinking about them.

I'd also say a lot of the credit belongs to timing rather than to us. The models had just become strong enough that natural language could serve as the medium for reasoning and planning. If I'd written the same paper two years earlier it wouldn't have worked, and if I'd written it two years later someone else would already have done it. When something that simple works, it usually means the field was ready for it.

So my honest assessment is that ReAct was less a shift in itself and more an early marker that the shift was happening, from treating these models as language models to treating them as agents. The real paradigm shift, if we want to use that word, is the one we're still in the middle of now, where the hard problems are environments, evaluation, and learning from interaction, rather than the prompting trick itself. I think of ReAct as the first sentence of that, not the whole paragraph.

r001.rationale: The response says the field is still in the middle of a shift, but does not suggest waiting five or ten years of hindsight to judge ReAct.

r002.rationale: It calls ReAct a simple prompting mechanism, but says nothing about academic norms making prompting research hard to accept.

r003.rationale: It discusses the research questions ReAct opened, but does not compare studying model use with training models as a way for academics to make a distinct contribution.

r004.rationale: It mentions timing and the models’ readiness, but not the risk of academic training research retracing discoveries made earlier by industrial labs such as OpenAI.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a paradigm shift. If you mean ReAct itself suddenly changed everything, that feels too strong. But if you mean it helped express a different way of using language models, then I think there is something there.

The distinction is between a model that produces an answer and a model that interacts with an environment. In the second case, it can reason about what to do, take an action, observe the result, and revise its next step. The answer doesn’t have to come entirely from what the model already knows; it can emerge through that interaction.

So I would assess it by whether that loop changes what systems can accomplish, and whether it becomes a useful foundation for later work. A better score on a benchmark is evidence of usefulness, but it isn’t enough to establish a paradigm shift.

My more modest interpretation is that ReAct made this direction clear and concrete. Whether you call it a paradigm shift is ultimately a judgment about the broader transition toward agents, rather than about one paper alone.

r003.rationale: It contrasts answering with interacting, but does not argue that studying model use was more valuable for academics than training models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a paradigm shift. If you mean ReAct itself fundamentally changed the capabilities of language models, I would be cautious about that claim. But if you mean a shift in how we use language models—from generating an answer in one pass to interacting with an environment—then I think it captures something important.

The core idea is to interleave reasoning and action. The model reasons about what to do, takes an action, observes the result, and then updates its next step. Its reasoning can guide its actions, and feedback from those actions can ground or correct its reasoning. That creates a loop rather than a single input-output mapping.

So I would assess it by whether that loop became a useful foundation for subsequent systems. Can the system gather information it doesn’t already have? Can it adjust when an action fails? Can it make progress on tasks where you cannot know the whole solution in advance? Those are more meaningful criteria than whether a particular prompt improves a benchmark score.

I’d describe ReAct as a simple formulation of that shift, rather than say one paper alone created a new paradigm.

r001.rationale: The response proposes evaluating ReAct by its usefulness to later systems, but does not say that judging its paradigm-shift status may require five or ten years of hindsight.

r003.rationale: It discusses how models are used, but does not argue that this focus could be more valuable for academics seeking a distinct contribution than training models.
